topic: The Mystery of Pi: Definition and History

sections.title: Hook: The Universal Constant
sections.content: Introduce Pi as a universal constant found in nature. Use a visual of a spinning bicycle wheel and a planet orbiting a star to show that regardless of size, circular objects share a mysterious secret ratio.
sections.example: A cat chasing a laser pointer in a circular path vs. a massive ferris wheel; both rely on the same geometric relationship.

sections.title: Definition: The Ratio of Circumference to Diameter
sections.content: Define π (Pi) as the ratio of a circle's circumference (C) to its diameter (d). Use an animation where a circle 'unrolls' along a flat line to measure its circumference against its diameter.
sections.example: If you have a circular pizza with a diameter of 10 inches, the crust (circumference) will always be exactly 10 × π inches long.

sections.title: Historical Evolution: From Estimation to Precision
sections.content: Briefly trace the timeline from the Babylonians and Egyptians (who approximated Pi as 3 or 3.125) to Archimedes' 'Method of Exhaustion,' where he drew polygons inside and outside a circle to trap the value of Pi.
sections.example: Visual of Archimedes increasing the number of sides on a polygon (from a hexagon to a 96-sided polygon) to 'squeeze' the circle and refine the decimal value.

sections.title: The Nature of Pi: Irrationality
sections.content: Explain that Pi is an 'irrational number,' meaning its digits go on forever without repeating. Contrast this with simple fractions like 1/4 to illustrate why π cannot be expressed as a perfect ratio.
sections.example: An animation showing a digital ticker-tape of Pi's digits (3.14159...) cascading infinitely down the screen, contrasting with a clean, static image of a square.

sections.title: Summary & Real-World Application
sections.content: Recap: Pi is the constant link between linear and circular measurement. Conclude by showing how Pi is used today in GPS technology and space exploration to calculate travel distances on curved planetary surfaces.
sections.example: A satellite orbiting Earth; Pi is the essential math 'fuel' that allows the satellite to calculate its precise path around the globe.
